title: Measured first: envpool, 4 PyTorch threads
text: envpool runs Breakout at about 4,000 agent steps/s with random actions (8-32 games), gymnasium's AsyncVectorEnv at 1,700-1,900, so envpool it is. The full PPO loop (8 games x 128 steps, 4 epochs x 4 minibatches, Nature CNN on CPU) runs at about 288 agent steps/s with 4 PyTorch threads, the same as with 6 and faster than with 8 (225: the CPU has 4 physical cores). 10 M frames = 2.5 M agent steps = about 2.4 hours, well inside the 12-hour budget, so no compiled port (ml-speedup) is needed. The update is 3/4 of the time.

title: Smoke test passed (10 minutes, with a crash-resume in the middle)
text: Two 5-minute halves: the second resumed from checkpoints/smoke/latest.pt at iteration 83 (340k frames) and continued to 655k frames. Checkpoints every 100k frames, MLflow metrics and the site files all written. Training score after 655k frames: about 2 per game, as expected this early (random play scores about 1.4).

title: Main run started: CleanRL settings, 10 M frames
text: Seed 1, 8 envs x 128 steps, 4 epochs x 4 minibatches of 256, clip 0.1, lr 2.5e-4 annealed linearly to 0, entropy 0.01, value coef 0.5, GAE lambda 0.95, gamma 0.99, grad norm 0.5. Episodic life and reward clipping for training only. Checkpoints every 500k frames; supervise.sh restarts from the last one after a crash.

title: Change 1: 10 M -> 40 M frames (CleanRL's '10M' means 10 M agent steps)
text: At 1.4 M frames the training score was flat at about 2 per game. Checking the plan against the sources found the problem: CleanRL's total_timesteps=10M counts agent steps, and with frame skip 4 that is 40 M frames, the same budget as the PPO paper (which reports 274.8 on Breakout at 40 M frames). The plan said 10 M frames, a quarter of that, with the learning rate annealed to 0 by then; at that budget CleanRL's own curves are around 100-150, far from 300. So the run was stopped at its 1.5 M checkpoint and resumed with --total-frames 40000000: same run, same MLflow run (the change is a tag there), and the linear learning-rate schedule now runs to 40 M (at 1.5 M frames the rate went from 2.16e-4 to 2.40e-4). At about 330 agent steps/s, 40 M frames take about 8 more hours, inside the 20-hour budget. Nothing else changed.

title: Change 2: goal checks now use two protocols
text: At 15 M frames the training games averaged about 150-190 points, but the goal check scored 86.5. Testing the 15 M model on the same 20 seeds both ways explained it: 184.8 with the standard training wrappers (a lost life is an episode boundary with envpool's soft reset and automatic FIRE; the score is still the real score of the whole 5-life game, exactly what the training curve counts) and 138.7 on plain full games, where nothing happens at a lost life and the agent must relaunch the ball itself. Both are common ways to report Atari scores, and the goal's 'standard Atari wrappers' fits the first. To avoid picking the flattering one, every checkpoint check from now on runs both protocols on the same seeds (12345-12354), the site shows both, and the final claim will say which protocol it is. The earlier checks were all strict full-game checks. Note also how noisy 10 games are: on 10 games the same 15 M model scored 86.5, on 20 games 138.7.

title: Correction: the protocol gap is mostly noise
text: A larger test of the 15 M model, 64 games per protocol on fresh seeds (777000+): 162.8 (standard error 13.1) with the training wrappers, 145.6 (standard error 14.8) on plain full games. The difference, about 17 points, is within the noise. The earlier 20-game comparison (185 vs 139) overstated it, and the 10-game goal check of 86.5 was simply a low draw. With a spread of about 110 points per game, a 10-game mean has a standard error of about 35 points. Both protocols stay in the goal checks. For the final goal, the model needs a true mean well above 300 to pass a 10-game check reliably.

title: Pre-registered: how the final result will be judged
text: Written at 20.5 M frames, before any final results exist. (1) Candidates: the final 40 M checkpoint and the best two checkpoints by the 10-game checks from 30 M frames on. (2) For each candidate, a 100-game evaluation on fresh seeds (900000-900099), strict full-game protocol, gives its true level; the candidate with the highest 100-game mean is THE model. (3) The goal check for THE model is 10 full games on seeds 12345-12354 (the fixed check seeds), strict full-game protocol; it is reported together with its 100-game mean, so a lucky 10-game draw can't pass silently. The training-wrapper protocol is reported alongside. (4) If THE model's 100-game mean is below 300, training continues from the 40 M checkpoint as change 3 (a short extra schedule), as long as the deadline allows, and every result is reported. Context for these rules: at 20 M frames the 10-game check said 229.7, but 64 envpool games said 169.5 (standard error 17), and 16 gymnasium games 132.4 (standard error 26.5): consistent with each other within the noise, and far noisier than one 10-game check suggests.

title: 30 M frames: first 10-game check above 300, true level still below
text: The fixed 10-game check (seeds 12345-12354, full game) of the 30 M checkpoint scored 332.7 (min 117, max 399); the training-wrapper protocol on the same seeds gave 223.1. 64 fresh full games (seeds 777000+) of the same model averaged 279.7 (standard error 14.7). By the pre-registered rules this is not the final result: the 10-game check is a lucky draw relative to the model's true level. True level by this measure: about 170 at 20 M, about 280 at 30 M.
